summary: Tulare sits on the dead-flat floor of the San Joaquin Valley, and the number that jumps out is a home-price-to-income ratio of roughly 4.3:1 — making homeownership at least arithmetically plausible at the median income, a rarity anywhere in California. That affordability has context: the city is a genuine job center for the southern Valley's massive dairy and agriculture industry, with major food-processing and cold-storage operations clustered in and around town, meaning many workers commute *into* Tulare rather than out of it. With 9.4 hours of daily sunshine on average and summer highs that routinely push well past 90°F, the climate is defined by relentless Central Valley heat from May through October and thick tule fog in winter — air conditioning isn't optional, and neither is patience on foggy Highway 99 mornings. The city's 20.8 square miles at a density of about 3,400 people per square mile produce a landscape of single-story subdivisions, big-box retail corridors, and agricultural land pressing right up against the city edge, with the snow-capped Sierra Nevada visible to the east on clear days. Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks sit roughly an hour's drive into those mountains, offering genuine alpine access that most Valley towns share but few appreciate enough. At its core, Tulare is a working agricultural city that happens to be in California — offering Valley-caliber affordability paired with Valley-caliber summers, fog, and air-quality tradeoffs.
